**Code.** Branch `phase1/planar` of `Symplectomorphism/c-gnn`: commits
`9261ece` (code and tests) and `af167f4` (compendium, Decision 9), Nov 7,
2026. The landing change below was accepted by Aykut the same day. Every
number on this page comes from
[`scripts/03_xiao_ji.py`](#reproduce), run on the current code and on
`84827c0`, the last commit before the change.

## In one paragraph

A contact state is a set of **principal contacts** (Xiao and Ji, *IJRR*
2001, Def. 1): contacts between surface elements that are not the boundary
of other contacting elements. Our earlier construction followed that
definition for the on-set but drifted from it elsewhere. Those drifts were
conveniences rather than needs, and they are gone. We keep only three
additions that their papers do not cover:

- **tolerances**, to recognize contacts in a simulator;
- **several bodies**, including a manipulator (the disk);
- **a no-contact state** for each pair of bodies.

## What changed

| | Before (`84827c0`) | Now (Decision 9) |
|---|---|---|
| Environment | Three convex bodies: floor, riser, platform. The step corner was *owned* by the riser, and the platform had an *open* end | One object E, a polygon. Its features are its edges (E:L, E:S, E:P) and its **convex** vertices, found from the geometry: only the step corner v<sub>S</sub> = E:S/P. The concave floor–riser junction is not a feature |
| Contacts per pair | At most one per body pair (convexity of each piece) | At most one per *convex element pair*, and none alongside a contact it contains (their Def. 8). The box can touch floor and riser at once |
| Transfers | Same or adjacent features on both sides: 92 pairs | Xiao–Ji containment only: one feature stays, the other is an edge and one of its own vertices. **56 pairs** |
| Compound edges | "Two transfers in different body pairs" | A set of single changes, all relaxing or all constraining (their Def. 9), kept only if every proper subset gives an invalid formation. On the step: the pivot and its reverse, 128 instances, as before |
| Hold gate | The contacts that persist through the edit | Statics of the edit's **less-constrained end**: the same contacts, now with a name and a precedent |
| Valid markings | 11,959 of 12,393 | 37,203 of 59,049 (several box–environment contacts at once) |

Of the 92 old transfer pairs, only 48 were Xiao–Ji neighbors. The other 44
were not:

- **20 went round a corner in one step.** Examples: the disk moving from
  −x<sub>B</sub> to −z<sub>B</sub>, or the box rolling from one edge onto
  the next.
- **24 changed both features at once**, which their Def. 10 excludes.

Each of these skips a contact state that the motion really passes through.
The disk now goes round a box corner in two transfers, through the
disk-on-vertex contact. That closes the open question "one Λ call or two".

## Why Xiao and Ji, and not something else

A literature search (three searches; 13 papers read in full against our
requirements) looked for a representation that is simpler and still meets
our needs:

- several bodies, including a nonconvex environment;
- one local transition per edge;
- recognizable from a pose with tolerances;
- encodable for a learner;
- extends to 3D;
- supports a statics test on the persisting contacts.

None qualified. Everything simpler is coarser, and everything more
principled is finer or impractical.

**Coarser: they cannot see the pivot.** A box tipping from its edge onto
its corner keeps the same label in all of these:

- **stances** of legged and climbing planners: a set of link–surface
  contacts with the location left continuous (Bretl 2006; Hauser, Bretl,
  Latombe, Harada and Wilcox 2008; Escande, Kheddar and Miossec 2013);
- **strata** of active contact constraints, per body pair (Kyaw and Kelly,
  arXiv 2608.15541, 2026) or per designated point (Goodwine and Burdick
  2002);
- **classes of free motion** (Paul and Ikeuchi 1995: 18 states in the
  plane, with no feature or body identity).

Kyaw and Kelly assume each stratum has dimension n − |A|. That fails here:
a box resting flat on its edge has a 1-dimensional set of poses, a box on
its corner a 2-dimensional one, and both have the same single active body
pair. With principal contacts as the label, the count comes out right.

**Finer: one motion becomes several edges.**

- The cells of the configuration-space obstacle, labeled by their active
  point constraints, split a single slide along the riser top into two
  edges.
- Kwak, Hasegawa and Chung (2011) triangulate every face, so their states
  depend on the triangulation.

**The Leuven precedent.** Meeussen et al. (*T-RO* 2007) use Xiao–Ji contact
formations as the discrete layer, with the graph software from Xiao's
group. They then break each principal contact into point contacts ("we use
the boundary points of the contacting area") for the force model, as
Lefebvre, Bruyninckx and De Schutter (*TRA* 2003) do. That two-layer
structure is ours too: principal contacts for the graph, and the endpoints
of each contact set for the hold LP. Their wrench models are frictionless;
ours has friction cones and motor limits.

## The hold gate's rule has a name

Multi-contact planners test the smaller stance at a transition. In Hauser
et al. (2008): at the transition the robot "can support itself only with
forces applied at the contact in [σ]", because "the applied force is zero
at the instant of time when the contact is made or broken". Hauser, Bretl
and Latombe (2005) already drop the moving hold from their classifier's
input, "since the force exerted at this hold during transition must be
zero". Escande et al. (2013) require "the stability constraints of the
smallest one" of the two stances.

Under Xiao–Ji's neighbor relation every edge links a formation to one it
contains, so "the less-constrained end" is always defined, and it equals
our persisting contacts. Step 2's choice 2 (use the old contact's normal)
now follows. In containment cases 2–3 the feature that defines the normal
is the one that stays.

## The landing changes

![The box near the step corner, labeled by the current code (+x to the left). Left: resting on the corner alone, {s<sub>v</sub>}. Middle: landed with +x<sub>B</sub> on the platform and overhanging the corner. v<sub>S</sub> is the end of the platform edge the box rests on, so the box's contact with v<sub>S</sub> is not principal, and the formation is {t}. Right: clear of the corner, still {t}.](media/xj_landing.svg){.lightbox}

Before, ownership turned both s<sub>v</sub> and t on after the landing, so
the landed box was {s<sub>v</sub>, t}. Under Xiao and Ji's Def. 1, v<sub>S</sub>
is a boundary element of the contacting platform edge, so s<sub>v</sub> is
not a principal contact there. The chain is one edit shorter:

{g} → {m<sub>x</sub>, g} → {m<sub>x</sub>, g, s} → *pivot* → {m<sub>x</sub>, g<sub>v</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>} → {m<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>} → *transfer(s<sub>v</sub> → t)* → {m<sub>x</sub>, t} → {t} → {m<sub>z</sub>, t} → *transport*.

**Two changes from the old chain:**

- **Landing is now a transfer.** It goes from the corner to the platform
  edge that the corner bounds.
- **Sliding off the corner is now transport.** It changes no contact.

**Support is unchanged.** t's contact set ends at the corner, so the landed
box is held exactly when its center of mass is over [0, x + a/2]. The
oracle test still agrees with the LP. `Cand` offers every step of the new
chain from a pose in its formation; the suite checks this.

## A caveat to carry into the paper: genericity

Xiao and Ji's theory assumes general position. They leave out degenerate
contacts because "these PCs have zero probability of occurrence in
practice". They also enter "state splitting", which needs two dimensions
to be exactly equal, by hand as exceptions. With tolerance bands, such
coincidences happen with real probability.

**How we handle it:**

- **Simultaneous changes.** Our rule for compound edges ("every proper
  subset is invalid") is the answer for simultaneous changes.
- **Ambiguous poses.** A pose the tolerances leave ambiguous (a tie) is
  refused as a node and as a solver success. Xiao (1993) treats such
  contacts as "inherently ambiguous" for the same reason.

**Ties rose under deep penetration.** On 4,000 jittered demo poses there
are now 475 ties (357 before):

- 474 of the 475 have a contact deeper than ε<sub>on</sub>;
- in 136 of them s<sub>v</sub> loses to t, the contact that contains it
  (median penetration 3.5 mm), where ownership used to turn both on.

The demo itself still has 2 tied frames of 1,721. This is the known issue
with ε<sub>pen</sub> = 10 mm, fixed in step 3; the test's budget is now 500.

## Checks

- The full suite, 68 tests, passes on Python 3.14, CPU (8:57) and GPU
  (13:46).
- **Gate equals persisting contacts.** For make, break, both transfer
  directions and the pivot, the gate's support points equal the persisting
  contacts.
- **Normals.** For g → g<sub>v</sub> and s → s<sub>v</sub>, the contained
  contact's normal equals the old contact's normal at the flush pose.
- **Compound edges, brute force.** A search over all sets of two or three
  single steps agrees with the implementation:
  - on every marking that has a compound edge;
  - on 1,500 random markings.

  Allowing up to four changes finds nothing new.

```bash
cd ~/repos/research/c-gnn && git switch phase1/planar && git pull && cd cmg
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv314/bin/python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/03_xiao_ji.py <out dir>
# the counts before Decision 9:
mkdir -p /tmp/old && git archive 84827c0 cmg | tar -x -C /tmp/old && cd /tmp/old/cmg
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu PYTHONPATH=src ~/repos/research/c-gnn/cmg/.venv314/bin/python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/03_xiao_ji.py --before
```
